what_its_for: Belatacept is a medicine that helps prevent your body from rejecting a transplanted kidney. It works by calming down your immune system so it does not attack the new kidney. It is used together with other medicines after a kidney transplant.
how_to_take: Belatacept is given as an IV infusion (a drip into your vein) by a nurse or doctor in a clinic or hospital. You will NOT give this medicine to yourself at home. Each infusion takes about 30 minutes. Always keep all of your infusion appointments.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose based on your body weight. You will usually receive infusions more often at first (on Day 1, Day 5, at the end of Weeks 2 and 4, then at the end of Weeks 8 and 12 after your transplant). After that, you will receive an infusion once every 4 weeks (once a month). Your doctor may adjust your schedule as needed.
missed_dose: If you miss or forget your infusion appointment, call your doctor or transplant clinic as soon as possible to reschedule. Do NOT skip doses or stop treatment without talking to your doctor first. Missing doses can put you at risk for kidney rejection.
storage: Belatacept is stored and prepared by healthcare professionals in a clinic or hospital. You do not need to store this medicine at home. After it is mixed, the infusion should be used within 24 hours and kept refrigerated (36°F to 46°F or 2°C to 8°C) until use.
what_to_avoid: Avoid being around people who are sick or have infections, as this medicine weakens your immune system. Avoid live vaccines (such as MMR, chickenpox, or nasal flu spray) while on this medicine — talk to your doctor before getting any shots. Limit your time in the sun and use sunscreen, since this medicine can increase your risk of skin cancer. Avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice unless your doctor says it is okay.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away if you notice: signs of infection such as fever, chills, sore throat, painful urination, or a cough that does not go away; signs of kidney rejection such as decreased urination, swelling, or pain over the transplant area; new lumps, bumps, or skin changes that worry you; confusion, memory problems, changes in speech, or weakness on one side of the body (these could be signs of a rare but serious brain infection called PML); any unusual bruising or bleeding; or if you feel very tired or unwell for no clear reason.
when_it_works: Belatacept starts working right away to protect your new kidney. However, you will need to keep taking it long-term, possibly for the rest of your life, to continue preventing rejection. Your transplant team will monitor your kidney function regularly with blood tests and check-ups.
special_populations: Pregnant or breastfeeding women: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. This medicine may harm an unborn baby, and it is not known if it passes into breast milk. Use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 8 weeks after your last dose. Children: Belatacept is NOT recommended for use in children or teenagers under 18 years old. Elderly patients: Older adults may use this medicine but should be monitored closely for infections and other side effects. People who have never had Epstein-Barr virus (EBV): If you have never been exposed to the Epstein-Barr virus, you have a higher risk of a serious condition called post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder (PTLD). Your doctor will check your EBV status before starting treatment.
